sources.title: Punish The Caro-Kann With The Advance Variation
Caro-Kann Advance search summary (Chessiverse, Lichess study, attackingchess; snippet only)

overview: After 3.e5 White gains space and fixes the centre; Black normally develops the light-squared bishop outside the chain with 3...Bf5 and then undermines the e5/d4 chain with ...c5 (often after ...e6), at times ...f6. White's set-ups range from the quiet Short System (Nf3, Be2, O-O, Be3 against ...c5) to aggressive kingside expansion with h4, g4 (Tal 4.h4, Bayonet 4.g4, Van der Wiel 4.Nc3 e6 5.g4, 4.Nf3 e6 5.Be2) aiming at a space and attack advantage. Typical positions are closed or semi-closed and French-like, with Black's bishop developed. It is the most popular way to fight the Caro-Kann in the 21st century and is double-edged: a space edge for White against a sound structure for Black.

white_ideas.idea: Short System: develop naturally with Nf3, Be2, O-O and answer ...c5 with Be3; a quiet, non-committal approach.
Aggressive kingside expansion with h4/g4 (Tal 4.h4, Bayonet 4.g4, Van der Wiel 4.Nc3 e6 5.g4), hunting the light-squared bishop and seeking attacking chances.
Space advantage from e5: restrain Black's pieces, use the d6 outpost and c4 break.
Main line 4.h4 h5 5.Bd3 for rapid development and Bg5; requires three or four precise theory moves from Black.

black_ideas.idea: Undermine White's centre with the ...c5 break (and sometimes ...f6).
Develop the light-squared bishop to f5 (or g4) before ...e6.
Control d5 as a strongpoint and delay castling to keep king flexibility.
Immediate 3...c5 (named Botvinnik-Carls by some sources, Arkell–Khenkin Variation in Wikipedia) strikes at once but costs a tempo.

typical_structures.structure: French-Advance-like pawn chain d4/e5 against c6/d5 with Black's bishop outside the chain; semi-closed centre where both sides manoeuvre.
After ...c5 and dxc5 or in the Short System, an open-ish centre with the d4 pawn under pressure.

character.notes: Mixed, depends on White's choice. The Short System is solid and positional; 4.h4, 4.g4 and 5.Bd3 lines are complex tactical battles. Modern Chess calls the variation 'double-edged', ranging from solid positional play to complex tactical battles. Wholesale Chess: moderately sharp, positional rather than tactical if Black knows theory. Wikipedia: the Caro-Kann overall has a solid reputation though tactical variations exist, and the Advance Variation lines are expanded aggressively by White.

gambit.notes: No gambit at the root. Gambit-like pawn sacrifices appear in some h4/g4 sub-lines (Modern Chess mentions potential gambits in 5.Bd3 lines).

soundness.notes: Sound for both. Modern Chess: positions favour White slightly because of space but Black reaches equality with precise play. Wholesale Chess: objectively sound for White (43% White wins at master level, in its dataset) and the most popular way to fight the Caro-Kann. Wikipedia: it became the most popular line in the 21st century despite being previously dismissed as inferior.

structure.notes: Closed or semi-closed: White's e5/d4 chain fixes the centre, Black attacks the base with ...c5; often compared to a French with Black's bishop outside. Search summary: results in a closed position where both parties manoeuvre pieces and Black aims for a pawn break eventually.

approach.notes: A standard main-line variation, not a system. Played widely at the top: Modern Chess names Dreev, Jobava and Vachier-Lagrave; Wikipedia says it became the most popular line in the 21st century; Firouzja and Ding Liren are named as players of the Caro-Kann in general.

level.notes: Studying Black's side. Substantial theory is needed in main lines: Modern Chess says three or four precise theoretical moves are essential in 5.Bd3 lines; Wholesale Chess says substantial study is necessary (Dreev's book, a 7+ hour video course). The Short System is lighter. Structurally it is clear (a French-like plan of ...c5), so the burden is mainly sharp-line theory rather than plans.

plan_phrases: light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain
kingside expansion with h4 and g4

sublines_that_differ.name: Tal Variation
sublines_that_differ.how: Aggressive kingside expansion; sharp and theory-heavy (4...h5 5.Bd3 main line).

sublines_that_differ.name: Botvinnik-Carls / Arkell–Khenkin Defence
sublines_that_differ.how: Black strikes immediately; avoids main-line theory, tactical, costs a tempo.

description.claim: The Advance Variation is highly strategic and combative, with White seizing a space advantage with 3.e5.
It creates a tense, semi-closed game.
description.note: Often closed with manoeuvring and a later pawn break.

description.claim: White aims to build a kingside attack.
description.note: Applies to the h4/g4 systems; the Short System is quieter.

description.claim: Black's primary goal is to undermine White's pawn chain, typically with the ...c5 break.

common_plans.claim: White: Build a kingside attack with Nf3, Be2, O-O, and sometimes g4-h4.
common_plans.note: Nf3/Be2/O-O is the Short System, which is quiet rather than an attack; g4/h4 are the aggressive systems.

common_plans.claim: Black: Prepare and execute ...c5. Develop the light-squared bishop to f5 or g4 before playing ...e6.
White: Restrain Black's queenside play and exploit the d4 square if Black plays ...c5.
common_plans.note: Nothing found stating this; d4 is White's own pawn square and the sources discuss the d4 base under attack, with the Be3 defence in the Short System. The claim looks garbled.

common_plans.claim: Black: Create queenside counterplay by targeting the d4 pawn and using the c-file.
common_plans.note: Pressure on d4 via ...c5 is supported; the c-file element is own understanding.
